questions.prompt: In September a boy's mother signs one form, and his name goes on the roll of an on-line high school. From that day on, every morning at nine, he sits down and connects his computer to the school's system. Which verb names what happened in September, and which names what happens at nine?

options.text: he enrolled in September, and he logs on every morning
he logged on in September, and he enrols every morning
he enrolled in September, and he enrols again every morning
he logged on in September, and he logs on again every morning

questions.explanation: Count how often each thing happens and the two verbs sort themselves out. Putting a name on the roll of a school is done once and holds until the pupil leaves: that is a decision, and the signed form is the whole of it. Connecting a machine so that today's lesson can reach it is done every morning, and undone the moment the connection drops: that is a gesture. Swap them and September becomes a morning like any other, while the nine o'clock connection becomes a new admission every day - a school whose twenty-two students would have to be admitted afresh before breakfast.

questions.prompt: At half past ten the corridor of an ordinary school fills up: three hundred pupils moving in every direction at once, bags, voices, everybody heading for the yard. Against the wall, three older boys are taking a smaller boy's lunch from him, as they do every day. Two words of this lesson name those two things. Which is which?

options.text: the crowd is the bustle, and what happens to the smaller boy is bullying
the crowd is the bullying, and what happens to the smaller boy is the bustle
the crowd is the bustle, and what happens to the smaller boy is a panic attack
both the crowd and what is being done to the smaller boy are bullying

questions.explanation: One of these two words blames nobody. A crowd of people moving about in a busy way is simply that: feet, noise, everybody going somewhere at the same moment, and there need not be a single unkind child in it. The other word is about intention, and it is one person deliberately frightening or hurting somebody weaker. Reverse the pair and you accuse three hundred pupils of a crime committed by three of them. Naming what the smaller boy feels rather than what is being done to him misses the question, which asked what happens, not how it is lived. And stretching the word that carries intention across the whole scene turns three hundred children hurrying to the yard into three hundred bullies.

questions.prompt: An on-line high school prints this day for its pupils: 0900, log on to the internet and chat to classmates in the "school hall"; 0930, classes start; 1030, break; 1100, Lesson 2; 1200, lunch; 1300, last class; 1400, "home time". Which of these lines could not stand on the timetable of a school with a building?

options.text: the nine o'clock line, where the day begins with a connection
the half past ten line, where the whole school stops for a break in mid-morning
the one o'clock line, where the last class of the day is due to begin
the twelve o'clock line, where the day stops for lunch

questions.explanation: Read the grid as a stranger would and almost every line of it is the day you already know: lessons that start, a pause in the middle of the morning, a meal at midday, one more class and then the end. All of that is printed in every school in the country. Only one line asks the pupils to reach their school by connecting a machine to the internet, and no building has ever needed such an instruction - its pupils arrive by walking through a gate. That single line is the entire difference between this school and yours, and it is set down as calmly as the bell.

questions.prompt: A mother is told that her son never works. She wants to answer that this is untrue, and to do it with the emphatic form, changing nothing else in the sentence "He works hard." Which sentence is correctly built?

options.text: He does work hard.
He does works hard.
He does to work hard.
He does working hard.

questions.explanation: Once the auxiliary is in place it takes charge of the person, so the verb behind it has nothing left to carry and stands in its plain form, the infinitive with no to in front of it. Leaving the ending on the verb makes two words claim the same job at once. Slipping a to between them turns the verb into something the auxiliary cannot govern here, and the ing form belongs to another construction altogether. The book's own example is built exactly like the sentence that works, and it is worth learning by heart for that reason.

questions.prompt: A pupil reads these ten words aloud, one after another: right, half, taught, friend, bustle, psychology, knowledge, comb, knee, through. He is told that all ten of them have one thing in common. What is it?

options.text: each of them is written with at least one letter that is not sounded
each of them is sounded exactly as the letters on the page are written
each of them begins with a letter that is not sounded
each of them holds two vowels standing side by side

questions.explanation: English keeps letters in its spelling long after it has stopped saying them, and every word on this list carries at least one: the gh of taught, the l of half, the i of friend, the t buried in bustle, the b at the end of comb. Claiming that these words are said letter for letter as they stand on the page is claiming the opposite of what the list was built to show. A silent letter at the start is true of only three of them, the ones opening on kn and ps, and a rule that covers three words out of ten is not what they have in common. As for two vowels together, half, comb, bustle and several others have nothing of the kind.
